general_notes: Gardiner 2025 anchors use the manuscript's printed page numbers, which are the PDF page minus 1 (PDF p. 1 is the cover page). The line numbers make every location unambiguous. I checked on that basis; only task 10's page was off.

Hampl 1995: I confirmed both problems the first reader reported. (1) Placebo age SD 19.6 is impossible with the printed range 18-55 and mean 48.4: the largest possible sample SD is about 14.5. The range also starts below the 20-year inclusion minimum. (2) Table IV prints plasma caffeine in mg per ml; the Discussion's comparison with a 5 mg/L threshold shows the values are in mg/L.

No extracted number was wrong. Every number was checked at its source, and every negative number on a rendered page. Most corrections are wording: naming the comparison group, writing 'no significant' instead of 'no change' or 'not correlated', putting back a hedge, or fixing a locator.

Other reporting errors seen (not used by any anchor): Rothman 2026 gives mean age 26.9 in the abstract and 26.3 in the text. Gardiner 2025 prints a REM-duration timing effect of +0.06 min with 95% CI -0.1 to 0 (p = 0.049). Gardiner 2023 prints the N3/N4 proportion change (-1.4%) with CI 0.2 to 2.6%.

results.note: All r and p values match the text and Fig. 8 (p. 16); the change correlations are positive on the image. 'Significantly' added to match 'absence of significant correlations'.

results.corrected_extracted: Water drunk was not significantly correlated with thirst before, during or after the walk (r = -0.028, p = 0.714; r = -0.001, p = 0.993; r = 0.059, p = 0.435) or with changes in thirst (r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046).
results.note: Values and minus signs checked on the rendered page (the text layer drops them). The paper reports no significant correlations, not no correlation.

plain.fix: short: People felt more anxious and low when hungover than when sober, and also described guilt. | but: The review does not say how big the changes were, and poor sleep or regret may explain part of them. | how 2: In most studies, people rated their mood when hungover and when sober or before drinking. | how 3: Most studies found worse mood when hungover, but two found no clear change in anxiety, at least for some people.
plain.note: Guilt comes from correlations with hangover severity and from interviews, not sober-day comparisons. The review reports no effect sizes, but the studies did measure. Surveys and interviews had no sober day. Table 4 says 'no significant', not 'no change'.

plain.fix: short: No study in the review tested a way to ease hangover worry; people said sharing the hangover with friends helped.
plain.note: The review only calls for intervention studies; it cannot show that no one has ever tested anything. Interviewees described bonding and sharing the hangover with friends. Other lines fit Table 1 (109 interviewed) and Table 5.

plain.fix: how 2: In most studies, the same people slept one night after alcohol and one night without it.
plain.note: 25 of 27 studies were crossover (lines 246-248). Other lines match: polysomnography in every study, REM later and shorter than control and worse with higher doses, and results that varied between studies.

plain.fix: short: On average, alcohol before bed did not help people fall asleep faster than on nights without alcohol. | how 4: In three of five studies, people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol.
plain.note: 'A drink' reads as one drink, which is an amount; the studies gave low to high doses and pooled them. 'Only after larger amounts' stays a finding, with no amount given.

plain.fix: short: No experiment had tested water for hangovers; by late morning thirst was no longer clearly above an alcohol-free day, but hangover was. | how 3: Students rated water as only modestly helpful, about 5 to 6 out of 10.
plain.note: Thirst was still reported at 15:30; it was just no longer significantly above the alcohol-free day (Fig. 5). Three non-experimental studies did look at water. Ratings were 5.2 to 5.8. The surveys are indeed the authors' own.

plain.fix: but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ. | how 1: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people. | how 2: Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter. | how 4: In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.
plain.note: The limitations name low to moderate habitual consumers, so 'rarely had caffeine' is wrong, and 'young men' is not stated. Some studies used home recordings, activity monitors or diaries. Wake after sleep onset is a duration. The paper does not link the perceived-wake studies to the measured waking.

plain.fix: how 2: Half got caffeine pills and half got identical dummy pills, and neither the patients nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which.
plain.note: The anaesthetist who filled the vials knew the allocation, so 'nobody knew' says too much. Other lines match Table V and the Methods.

plain.fix: short: In one small trial, fewer patients given caffeine pills had headaches after surgery than patients given dummy pills. | how 2: Nurses gave either caffeine pills or identical dummy pills around the operation. | how 3: The amount and acidity of stomach fluid, which caffeine can raise, did not differ significantly between the groups.
plain.note: The pills were given before any headache, so 'stopped' overstates what was prevention. A ward nurse gave them (Methods). Table IV reports non-significant differences, not equal values.
